commitResults.messageTitle: Set up Checkstyle and fix violations it found
commitResults.messageBody:
Adds the Gradle checkstyle plugin wired to AB3's checkstyle.xml/
suppressions.xml, which enforces the se-edu coding standard
automatically instead of relying on manual review.

Fixes the violations it caught on the existing codebase: six files
were missing a trailing newline, and three assertThrows lambdas in
ParserTest wrapped the line so that '(' started the continuation line
instead of ending the previous one; joining them onto one line (they
fit under 120 chars) resolves that.

`./gradlew checkstyleMain checkstyleTest` now passes with zero
violations.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add JavaFX GUI with a Spider-Man theme (Level 10)
commitResults.messageBody:
Follows Parts 1-4 of the se-edu JavaFX tutorial, built straight to the
Part 4 FXML architecture: Launcher/Main load MainWindow.fxml, which is
controlled by MainWindow and shows chat bubbles built by DialogBox.

Refactors Ui to return response strings instead of printing them
directly, and adds Peter#getResponse/getWelcomeMessage/getLoadingMessage/

spokes and rings) rather than any Marvel-owned character artwork.

commitResults.messageTitle: Use Streams to replace manual loops over tasks (A-Streams)
commitResults.messageBody:
Replace hand-written for-loops that filter, transform, or collect over
a list of tasks with the equivalent Stream pipeline, where doing so
keeps or improves readability:

- TaskList.getTasksOnDate / findTasks: filter the task list with a
  predicate instead of manually building up a result list.
- Storage.load: map each saved line to a Task and drop the malformed
  ones (map + filter(Objects::nonNull)) instead of a loop with a
  null-check and manual add.
- Storage.save: map each task to its storage line instead of a loop
  that appends to a list.
- Ui.showTaskList / showFoundTasks: number and join each task's display
  line with IntStream + Collectors.joining instead of a StringBuilder
  loop.
- Ui.showTasksOnDate: prefix and join each task's display line with
  stream().map(...).collect(joining(...)) instead of a StringBuilder
  loop.

Each change is behaviour-preserving (verified by the existing
TaskListTest and ParserTest suites, which still pass) and was chosen
because the loop body was a straightforward filter/map/collect with no
mid-loop side effects beyond building the result - exactly the shape
Streams are meant for. Loops with genuine side effects elsewhere in the
codebase (e.g. Ui.readCommand, Storage.ensureDataFileExists) were left
alone, since forcing those into a Stream would trade a clear loop for
a stream used only for its side effects, which is discouraged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract addTaskAndRespond helper to remove duplication in handleCommand (A-CodeQuality)
commitResults.messageBody:
The TODO, DEADLINE, and EVENT cases in Peter.handleCommand each ended
with the exact same three statements: add the parsed task to the list,
persist the list to storage, and return the task-added confirmation
message. Introduce a private addTaskAndRespond(Task) helper that
performs this shared sequence once, and have each of the three cases
call it with their own parsed task instead.

This is the highest-priority issue found when reviewing the code
against the CS2103 code quality guidelines
(https://nus-cs2103-ay2627-s1.github.io/website/se-book-adapted/chapters/codeQuality.html):

- SLAP ("maintain a single level of abstraction"): the three cases
  mixed command-specific parsing with the generic add/persist/respond
  sequence in the same block. Each case now stays at one level by
  delegating the generic part to a named helper.
- Avoid Long Methods ("ideally under 30 lines"): handleCommand dropped
  from about 55 lines to about 40, closer to the guideline's target.

It also removes an implicit coupling: previously, changing the
add/persist/respond sequence meant remembering to update it in three
separate places; now there is a single place to change.

Verified with the existing ParserTest and TaskListTest suites (still
pass, since this only reshapes handleCommand without changing
behaviour) and Checkstyle (clean).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add assertions to document internal invariants (A-Assertions)
commitResults.messageBody:
Add `assert` statements at points where a violated condition would
indicate a programming bug rather than invalid user input (user input
is already validated and reported via PeterException, and stays that
way - assertions are not used as a substitute for that). Each one
documents an assumption the surrounding code already relies on:

- Task(String): the description passed in should never be null; every
  caller (Todo/Deadline/Event constructors, all fed by Parser after an
  emptiness check) already guarantees this.
- Command.fromKeyword(String): the keyword should never be null; its
  only caller, Parser.parseInput, always derives it from
  String.split(...)[0], which cannot return null.
- Parser.parseInput(String): rawInput should never be null; both the
  CLI (Ui.readCommand) and the GUI input path only ever pass a
  non-null line.
- TaskList(List<Task>): the loaded task list should never be null;
  its only caller passes Storage.load()'s result directly, which is
  documented to always return a (possibly empty) list.
- Event(String, LocalDateTime, LocalDateTime): the end time should not
  be before the start time. This documents an intended domain
  invariant; Parser.parseEvent does not yet enforce it on user input,
  so this also flags a gap to close later rather than a fully
  guaranteed precondition.
- Storage.createTask(String[], String): parts should have at least 3
  elements; its only caller, parseTask, already checks this before
  calling it, so the assertion documents that the two methods must be
  kept in sync.

Gradle's `test` task runs with assertions enabled by default, so these
are exercised on every test run; verified the existing ParserTest and
TaskListTest suites still pass with them in place, and Checkstyle is
clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
A-Assertions: document internal invariants with assert
A-CodeQuality: extract addTaskAndRespond to remove duplication
A-Streams: use Streams for task collection processing

commitResults.messageTitle: Rename `on` to `schedule` and order results as deadlines then events (BCD-Extension)
commitResults.messageBody:
Renames the date-lookup command from `on` to `schedule`, and changes
what it returns from an unordered mix of matching tasks to an actual
schedule: deadlines due that day first (sorted by due time), followed
by events starting that day (sorted by start time).

Why:
- `on <date>` answered "what's happening on this date" but the name
  didn't say so, and the result order was just insertion order (the
  order tasks were originally added), not the order they'd actually
  occur in - which is what you want from something calling itself a
  schedule.
- Grouping deadlines before events, each sorted chronologically within
  its group, is a deliberate, simple ordering rather than a single
  merge-by-time sort across both types: deadlines and events answer
  different questions ("due by" vs "happening from"), so keeping them
  visually separated avoids implying they're on one continuous
  timeline when a deadline's time isn't really a scheduled slot the
  way an event's is.

What changed:
- Command.ON -> Command.SCHEDULE.
- Peter.handleCommand's `case ON` -> `case SCHEDULE`, now calling the
  renamed TaskList/Ui methods below.
- TaskList.getTasksOnDate -> TaskList.getScheduleForDate: builds the
  deadline and event matches as two separately-sorted lists
  (Comparator.comparing(Deadline::getBy) /
  Comparator.comparing(Event::getFrom)) and concatenates them, instead
  of a single filter pass that preserved insertion order.
- Ui.showTasksOnDate -> Ui.showSchedule: message copy now talks about
  a "schedule" instead of what Peter "dug up".
- Parser's javadoc for parseDate updated to reference the `schedule`
  command instead of `on`.
- TaskListTest: renamed the existing tests to match, and added
  getScheduleForDate_multipleDeadlinesAndEvents_sortsEachGroupChronologically,
  since the original test only had one deadline and one event and so
  couldn't actually prove either the deadlines-before-events grouping
  or the within-group chronological order - both of which are the
  actual point of this change. Also strengthened the existing
  matching-deadline-and-event test to assert exact list equality
  (deadline then event) instead of just checking membership. Removed
  the now-unused assertFalse import.

Verified with the full test suite and Checkstyle (./gradlew check),
plus a manual run against a scratch data file (not the real
data/duke.txt): after adding a deadline and an event on the same date,
`schedule <date>` returned the deadline first, then the event, and
`on <date>` was correctly unrecognised.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Merges the BCD-Extension increment: renames the `on <date>` command to
`schedule <date>`, and changes its result from an unordered mix of
matching tasks into an actual schedule - deadlines due that day first
(sorted by due time), followed by events starting that day (sorted by
start time).

See branch-BCD-Extension's commit (tagged BCD-Extension) for the full
rationale and list of changes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Polish the GUI: asymmetric layout, error highlighting, resizable window
commitResults.messageBody:
Reworks the JavaFX GUI along several of the polish ideas from the iP
brief (i, ii, iii, iv, v, vi), chosen because they reinforce each
other rather than being independent tweaks:

i. Asymmetric conversation layout
   Peter's replies no longer mirror the user's chat bubble with a
   flipped avatar. The user's input is a narrow bubble on the right;
   Peter's replies are a wide response panel on the left with a red
   accent border instead of a bubble shape. The conversation is
   between a person and an app, not two people, so treating both
   sides identically (just mirrored) was the wrong metaphor.

ii. Error highlighting
   Previously every reply - success or PeterException error - used
   the same red bubble, so a typo'd command looked identical to a
   normal confirmation. Peter.getResponse now returns a
   Peter.Response(text, isError) record instead of a bare String, and
   MainWindow picks DialogBox.getErrorDialog (amber accent, amber
   text, dark amber background) instead of getPeterDialog whenever
   isError is true. The startup "couldn't load saved tasks" message
   gets the same treatment via the new Peter.isLoadingError().

v. + vi. Profile pictures
   Removed both avatars entirely rather than tweaking their shape.
   There are only ever two fixed participants (the user and Peter),
   and bubble side + colour already disambiguate them instantly, so a
   99x99 face repeated on every single line was pure visual noise -
   worse, it ate about a quarter of the window's width on every
   message in an app whose replies are often multiple lines of text
   in a narrow 400px-wide window. Deleted the now-unused
   resources/images/User.png; Peter.png stays only as the window/
   taskbar icon (Main.java), not a per-message avatar.

iii. Space and padding
   With the avatar column gone, widened the usable text area (user
   bubbles ~72% of width, Peter panels ~94%), added consistent
   spacing between messages (VBox spacing via #dialogContainer) and
   slightly more generous label padding, since the freed-up space
   needed accompanying breathing room to read as intentional rather
   than a re-centred bug.

iv. Resizable window
   Removed stage.setResizable(false) and the AnchorPane's
   maxWidth/maxHeight="-Infinity" lock in MainWindow.fxml, both of
   which hard-pinned the window to exactly 400x600. Replaced the
   TextField/Button/ScrollPane's fixed layoutX/Y positions with
   AnchorPane anchors on all relevant sides so they track the window
   edges, added fitToWidth to the ScrollPane, and bound each dialog
   label's max width to a fraction of its own (now parent-tracking)
   width so wrapped text reflows correctly as the window is resized
   instead of clipping or staying a fixed pixel width. The stage
   keeps its existing 400x600 minimum size.

Also added PeterTest to cover the new Response/isLoadingError
behaviour (the existing suite had no tests touching Peter itself), and
manually verified the whole window loads and both opening dialogs
render via a throwaway JavaFX-toolkit smoke test (Platform.startup +
FXMLLoader against the real MainWindow.fxml/main.css), since JUnit
alone can't catch FXML/CSS wiring mistakes (missing fx:id, bad
resource paths). That smoke test was deleted after use, per this
repo's convention for one-off manual-verification tests.

These design choices (dropping avatars, panel-vs-bubble asymmetry) are
my own reasoning from the brief's prompts, not adopted from a specific
past iP showcase project.

Verified with ./gradlew check (JUnit + Checkstyle), both passing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Merges the GUI polish increment: asymmetric conversation layout
(Peter's replies as a wide response panel instead of a mirrored
bubble), amber-accented error highlighting via the new
Peter.Response(text, isError) record, removal of the per-message
profile-picture avatars in favour of alignment/colour to disambiguate
speakers, tightened padding/spacing, and a genuinely resizable window
with anchors that let the layout reflow.

See branch-GUI-Polish's commit for the full rationale.

commitResults.messageTitle: Give Peter a coherent friendly-neighbourhood-Spider-Man personality
commitResults.messageBody:
The app already had a Spider-Man-coded GUI (red/blue colours,
web-pattern background, "PETER" banner, from the Level-10 and
GUI-Polish work) but the phrase library talked like a completely
different character - a mole or archivist digging through old notes
("dug up your tasks", "the drawer got stuck", "a scribbled-on line").
Spiders don't dig, they web-sling; the visual and textual halves of
the bot's identity were pulling in different directions instead of
being one cohesive personality.

Kept the name Peter (Peter Parker) and the existing GUI colour scheme,
since both already pointed the right way and rewriting them would
just be throwing away working design for no reason. Rewrote every
user-facing phrase instead:

- Ui.java: every showX() message now uses web-slinging language
  ("webbed that one up", "stuck to the web", "swung by the archive")
  and addresses the user the way Spider-Man actually talks ("pal",
  "hero", "bud"), including an explicit "friendly neighbourhood"
  callback in the welcome message to make the identity unambiguous
  rather than only implied by colour.
- Parser.java: rewrote the three error phrases (missing arguments,
  invalid date, invalid date/time) to "spidey-sense" language. Also
  extracted the missing-arguments message, previously the literal
  string "yea you're gonna have to give me more than that buddy."
  duplicated 7 times across parseInput/parseTodo/parseFindKeyword/
  parseDeadline/parseEvent/parseTaskIndex, into a single
  MISSING_ARGUMENTS_MESSAGE constant - fixing a DRY violation flagged
  in an earlier code-quality review while touching this text anyway.
- Storage.java: rewrote the load-failure, save-failure, and
  skipped-line warning messages.
- Peter.java: rewrote the unrecognised-command message.
- Main.java: window title now reads "Peter - Your Friendly
  Neighbourhood Task Manager" instead of just "Peter", since that's
  user-visible (taskbar/title bar) and costs nothing to make explicit.

No GUI/CSS/FXML changes: the colour palette, web-pattern background,
and banner already embodied this personality, so touching them would
have been busywork rather than a fix.

No existing test asserts on exact message wording (checked before
starting), so nothing broke; verified with ./gradlew check (JUnit +
Checkstyle, both passing) and a throwaway test that printed every
message end-to-end through Peter.getResponse to read the new voice in
context before committing (deleted after use, per this repo's
convention for one-off manual-verification tests).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Merges the personality increment: keeps the name Peter and the
existing Spider-Man-themed GUI, and rewrites every user-facing message
to an actual friendly-neighbourhood-Spider-Man voice instead of the
mismatched mole/archivist phrasing it had before. Also extracts the
7x-duplicated missing-arguments error string into a single constant.

See branch-Personality's commit for the full rationale.

commitResults.messageTitle: Handle the error categories the product will actually encounter
commitResults.messageBody:
Audited the app against three categories of anticipated errors
(command format, environment/file, and unexpected data) and fixed
five confirmed real bugs, plus added robustness the brief specifically
asked for. Each fix below was verified with a scratch reproduction
before changing anything, not assumed.

Confirmed bugs fixed:

1. Non-existent calendar dates were silently accepted. Verified:
   LocalDate.parse("2019-02-30", DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("yyyy-MM-dd"))
   returns 2019-02-28 instead of throwing, because the default
   ResolverStyle.SMART clamps invalid dates instead of rejecting them.
   Switched Parser's and Storage's date/time formatters to
   ResolverStyle.STRICT. That alone broke valid parses too (STRICT
   can't resolve a bare "yyyy" year-of-era field without an explicit
   era), so also switched the pattern from yyyy to uuuu (proleptic
   year) - the standard fix for this specific java.time gotcha.
   Verified both the fix and the fix-for-the-fix with a scratch
   reproduction before changing the real formatters.

2. Leading whitespace before a command broke parsing entirely.
   Verified: "  todo read book".split(" ", 2)[0] returns "" (empty
   string), so the whole line was misparsed as an unrecognised
   command instead of a todo. Parser.parseInput now trims the whole
   raw input first and splits on any whitespace run (\s+) rather than
   a single literal space, which also makes it robust to tabs.

3. An event's end time being before or equal to its start time was
   never actually enforced - only documented with an `assert`, which
   is disabled by default at runtime (Gradle's test task happens to
   run with -ea, masking this in tests, but `gradlew run` and the
   packaged jar do not). Parser.parseEvent now checks
   to.isAfter(from) and throws PeterException before constructing the
   Event; Storage.createTask applies the same check to a loaded line
   and treats a violation as malformed (skip + warn), consistent with
   how it already handles every other structural problem. Strengthened
   Event's assert message to reflect that the invariant is now
   actually guaranteed by both callers, not just documented as a gap.

4. A description containing '|' (Peter's storage field delimiter) or a
   line break silently corrupted the save file: it would be written
   with extra '|'-delimited fields, then silently dropped on the next
   load because the field count no longer matched. Parser now rejects
   such descriptions at the todo/deadline/event command level, before
   a Task is ever constructed.

5. No duplicate-task detection existed at all - adding the same task
   twice just added it twice. Added content-based equals/hashCode to
   Task (type + description) and its subclasses Deadline (+ due time)
   and Event (+ start/end time), deliberately excluding completion
   state so marking a task done doesn't change what counts as a
   duplicate of it. TaskList.add now throws PeterException on an exact
   duplicate; Peter.addTaskAndRespond propagates it. Only add() - not
   the constructors used to load from storage - enforces this, so
   pre-existing duplicates in an old save file still load rather than
   crashing startup.

Robustness added (not crashes, but explicitly requested in the
brief's "multiple spaces" and "parameter specified multiple times"
examples):

- Deadline/event date-time text is now whitespace-normalised (extra
  internal spaces collapsed to one) before parsing, so e.g.
  "2019-12-02  1800" parses the same as "2019-12-02 1800" instead of
  failing on a stray space.
- A /by, /from, or /to marker specified more than once is now
  rejected with a specific message, instead of silently being parsed
  as part of the date/time text (which previously just produced a
  generic "invalid date" error - not a crash, but not a helpful one).

Also fixed a message I missed in an earlier personality pass:
TaskList's out-of-range index message was still in the old
mole/archivist voice ("that task doesn't exist buddy") instead of the
current spidey voice.

Verified environment/file handling already in place and left
unchanged: Storage.load/save already catch IOException broadly
(covers a missing file, a missing parent directory via
FileAlreadyExistsException, and permission errors), and
Storage.parseTask already skips and warns on a malformed line (wrong
field count, invalid status marker, unparseable date, unknown type
code) rather than crashing. Added StorageTest, which had zero prior
coverage, to lock this behaviour in and cover the new date/event
checks against actual file I/O rather than just in-memory objects.

Added 25 new tests across ParserTest (whitespace handling, duplicate
markers, non-existent dates, description validation, event ordering),
TaskListTest (duplicate detection, including that marking a task done
doesn't exempt it from the check), and the new StorageTest (missing
file/directory, malformed lines, the new date/event checks, and a
save-then-load round trip). Verified with ./gradlew check (68 tests,
all passing; Checkstyle clean) and a throwaway end-to-end test that
ran every new scenario through Peter.getResponse against a scratch
data file to read the actual user-facing behaviour before committing
(deleted after use, per this repo's convention).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Merges the error-handling increment: fixes 5 confirmed bugs (silently
accepted non-existent dates, leading-whitespace command parsing
breaking entirely, unenforced event end-after-start invariant,
save-file corruption from '|'/newline in a description, no duplicate-
task detection), plus whitespace normalisation and duplicate-marker
rejection for date/time arguments. Adds StorageTest (previously zero
coverage) and 25 new tests overall.

See branch-ErrorHandling's commit for the full rationale and how each
bug was verified before being fixed.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add JUnit tests to cover nearly all automatable code
commitResults.messageBody:
Audited every non-GUI class for test coverage. Command, Task, Todo,
Deadline, Event, Ui, and PeterException had zero dedicated tests
(only exercised incidentally through Parser/TaskList tests, which
never touched several of their methods at all - e.g. no test anywhere
called Task.markAsNotDone, Deadline.toFileFormat, or
Command.fromKeyword directly). Storage's actual IOException
catch-branches in load()/save() were never exercised - the existing
"missing parent directory" test only covered the success path of
creating one. Peter.run(), the CLI session loop, had zero coverage.

Added:
- TaskTest, TodoTest, DeadlineTest, EventTest: direct coverage of
  markAsDone/markAsNotDone, getStatusIcon, toFileFormat, toString
  (including the midnight-omission formatting logic, tested
  independently for each end of an Event's range), and the
  equals/hashCode contract added in the error-handling pass -
  including that completion state is ignored and that same-description
  different-type tasks are not equal (Task vs Todo, Deadline vs Todo).
  EventTest also verifies the end-after-start invariant is genuinely
  enforced by asserting the constructor throws AssertionError for a
  non-after end time (Gradle's test task runs with -ea).
- CommandTest: keyword recognition, case-insensitivity, and the
  unrecognised-keyword fallback to UNKNOWN.
- PeterExceptionTest: the message is preserved through the exception.
- UiTest: every showX() message-building method, plus readCommand()
  and close() via System.in redirection (restored in @AfterEach so it
  can't leak into other tests).
- StorageTest: two new IOException-path tests - the data file itself
  being a directory, and its parent path being blocked by an existing
  regular file - covering load()'s throw-PeterException branch and
  save()'s print-a-warning-and-continue branch, neither of which any
  existing test actually triggered. Both verified empirically to throw
  IOException on this platform before being relied on (directory
  handling can be surprising across platforms).
- PeterTest: isLoadingError()=true via the same directory-as-data-file
  trick (and that the app still starts with an empty list rather than
  refusing to run), bye/isExit() coverage, and a full run() session
  test that redirects System.in/System.out, feeds a scripted
  ["todo read book", "bye"] session, and asserts on the actual printed
  transcript - exercising the CLI loop, Ui.readCommand/close, and
  Peter.getResponse together rather than each in isolation.

Deliberately left untested, per the brief's own carve-out: DialogBox,
MainWindow, Main, and Launcher, all of which require a live JavaFX
Stage/Scene to exercise meaningfully - these were verified manually
(and the throwaway JavaFX-toolkit smoke test from the GUI-polish
pass). A full manual pass across different OSes, screen resolutions,
and OS-language settings (the brief's other suggestion) is still worth
doing separately, though one relevant risk is already mitigated in
code: Deadline/Event's display formatters are pinned to
Locale.ENGLISH, so date rendering doesn't change with the OS locale
the way an unpinned formatter's would.

68 new tests added (68 -> 136 total). Verified with ./gradlew check:
all passing, Checkstyle clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Merges the test-coverage increment: adds dedicated tests for every
non-GUI class that had none (Command, Task, Todo, Deadline, Event, Ui,
PeterException), plus previously-unexercised IOException paths in
Storage and a full run() session test for Peter. 68 new tests
(68 -> 136 total). GUI classes (DialogBox, MainWindow, Main, Launcher)
deliberately left untested, per the brief's own carve-out - verified
manually instead.

See branch-MoreTests's commit for the full rationale.

commitResults.messageTitle: Purge remaining "Duke" references; ensure Peter is shown consistently
commitResults.messageBody:
The GUI itself (title bar, banner) and CLI banner were already fully
rebranded to Peter from earlier work, but a full repo-wide audit
(grep -rni "duke" across all source/config/doc files) turned up four
places still named after the original template:

- build.gradle: shadowJar's archiveFileName was 'duke.jar' - the
  actual file a user downloads and runs would have been called
  duke.jar, the most directly user-facing leftover of the lot. Now
  'peter.jar'.
- Peter.java: DATA_FILE_PATH defaulted to "./data/duke.txt". Not
  GUI-visible, but still a literal "Duke" footprint the running
  product leaves on disk. Now "./data/peter.txt". This repo's local
  (gitignored) data/duke.txt was copied to data/peter.txt so existing
  local task data still loads under the new default path rather than
  being silently orphaned - confirmed with the user first, since this
  affects real saved data, not just source.
- README.md: the "expected output" ASCII banner shown in the IntelliJ
  setup instructions was still the original Duke figlet banner - this
  wasn't just branding, it was stale documentation that no longer
  matched what the app actually prints (Ui.java's banner was already
  customized to spell "Peter" with a different welcome message).
  Replaced with the real current output. Also softened the "named
  after the Java mascot Duke" sentence to make clear the product has
  since been renamed, rather than reading as if Duke were still the
  current name.
- docs/README.md: removed a leftover "// Update the title above to
  match the actual product name" instruction comment - the title was
  already updated to "Peter User Guide", so the comment was stale and
